 Swimming is one of the few times you can't take your phone along for the ride. At least, not if you want it to survive. Bluetooth signals don't travel well underwater, so swimming headphones need another way to play your music, usually through built-in storage or a dedicated underwater transmitter.
 Most of the headphones in this guide use bone conduction, sending sound through your cheekbones rather than into your ears. It's a handy design for swimming, and it means you can often use the same pair for a run or bike ride on dry land. The Zygo Z2 takes a different approach, using a dedicated transmitter to stream audio underwater without needing to load tracks onto the headphones first.
 We've tested these headphones in and out of the water, and not every pair makes the cut. We look for a secure, comfortable fit that won't have you fiddling with your headphones halfway through a length, alongside sound quality that makes your playlist worth listening to. Every pick is rated IPX7 or above, meaning it's designed to handle submersion rather than just a bit of rain.
 Still not sure about waterproof vs water-resistant headphones ? Read our full explainer. Waterproof means submersion, while water resistance means withstanding slashes, sweat, and rain. We have a dedicated guide for the best bone conduction headphones too.
 Back to swimming, our favourite headphones are the Shokz OpenSwim Pro , but there are other pairs worth considering depending on where you swim and how you like to listen. Here's how our full lineup compares.

 How to choose the best swimming headphones for you 
 First off, you need to check the headphones' IP code. IP, which stands for 'ingress protection'. The two-digit IP scale rates a device for waterproofing and dustproofing.
 A rating of 0-6 for the first digit indicates protection against solid particles, with anything above 6 being rated 'X' – effectively impervious. The second indicates protection against liquid ingress, rated from 0-9. A score of 7 is the first number on the scale qualifying the device for total immersion in water, therefore 'IPX7' is the code to look out for.
 The style you prefer is also worth considering when buying a pair of waterproof earbuds or headphones. If you like the fit and feel of regular in-ear headphones, a couple of earbuds might be your best bet. However, a pair of bone-conducting headphones will work best if you want to keep your ears free to tune into your environment.
 It's also worth thinking about how you want to access your music. If you want to keep your phone by the side of the pool, regular Bluetooth earbuds just won't cut it underwater.
 If you don't want to rely on your phone, you'll need a pair of swimming headphones with a built-in MP3 player. You'll just need to be sure to look into how much storage you're getting. For example, the Nank Runner Diver2 Pro headphones in our guide above have an onboard MP3 player with 32GB worth of storage – that's (very roughly) around 8,000 MP3s.
 How we test the best swimming headphones 
 We've tested every pair of swimming headphones in this list and in order for them to be included in this very select and specific roundup, we needed each pair of headphones to excel at a number of things.
 The first thing, of course, is effective waterproofing – you need these swim-specific headphones to survive multiple dunks in the drink. But that is closely followed by audio performance, battery life, wearer security, comfort and ease of use. An IPX7 rating should not mean poor sound quality and we made sure to check for that.
 From there, we looked at Bluetooth connectivity – or alternatives to it, such as onboard storage or (anyone familiar with smartphones knows that generally, they don't play well with water) or FM radio transmitters. Elsewhere, on-device controls, comfort, value for money and of course decent sound quality helped us to reach our verdicts.
 Our testing is independent – there are no sales teams involved in our review process. That is why if you take the plunge (see what we did there?) and buy a set of waterproof headphones from this buying guide, you can rest assured you're purchasing a TechRadar-approved product. For more information, you can check out our page on how we test . Happy shopping – and safe swimming.
 FAQs 
 Can you use Bluetooth headphones while swimming?
 The short answer is, no, not reliably.
 The longer answer, Bluetooth uses radio signals that water quickly weakens and scatters, so the connection between your phone or watch and headphones usually drops once you submerge. That is why most swim-specific headphones use built-in MP3 storage for underwater listening: load music, podcasts or audiobooks before your session, then switch to their offline mode in the water.
 Bluetooth is still useful on dry land for running, walking and taking calls. If you want to avoid loading files, the Zygo Z2 takes a different approach, receiving audio from a dedicated transmitter placed poolside. 
Our advice? Check the device instructions before relying on a watch-and-headphones combination, as support varies.
 What IP rating do I need for swimming headphones?
 Look for at least IPX7 if you want headphones for swimming. IP means Ingress Protection and the two characters after it refer to separate tests: the first is for solid objects and dust, while the second is for water. In IPX7, the “X” means no dust rating is stated and the “7” is the water rating, indicating protection against temporary immersion.
 Take the Shokz OpenSwim Pro as an example, its IP68 rating means it has a dust rating of 6 and a water rating of 8. It does not mean “better than IPX7” by adding 6 and 8 together. The water rating is the key figure for swimmers, and a higher number can mean stronger protection, but the manufacturer’s own limits still matter. Our review states the OpenSwim Pro is rated for depths of up to two metres for up to two hours.
 Are bone-conduction headphones good for swimming?
 Waterproof bone-conduction headphones are well suited to swimming if you want to keep your ears open and hear your surroundings, but not every bone-conduction model is rated for submersion. Check its IP rating and the manufacturer’s stated swimming limits before getting in the water. Rather than sealing the ear canal with a speaker, bone-conduction models transmit sound through vibrations against the cheekbones. That can be more comfortable for some swimmers and makes it easier to notice poolside instructions or ambient sounds.
 The trade-off is that they generally cannot match conventional in-ear headphones for bass, detail or isolation. Most picks in this guide use bone conduction, while the Zygo Z2 differs chiefly in how it receives audio. Its dedicated poolside transmitter sends a signal to the headset, avoiding the need to load MP3 files before hopping in the pool.
 Should I choose swimming headphones with MP3 storage or a poolside transmitter?
 Choose MP3 storage if you want the simplest, most portable solution for pool and open-water swims. Choose a poolside transmitter if you mainly swim in a pool and want to listen without managing audio files. Built-in storage works without a nearby phone because the music is on the headphones themselves, but you will need to transfer compatible files before you swim.
 A transmitter-based option such as the Zygo Z2 can stream audio from the pool edge and add coaching features, but the transmitter needs to stay nearby, which makes it less practical for open water. It's also worth checking whether any subscription features are required before buying.
 Can you swim with Apple AirPods?
 No, Apple AirPods are not designed for swimming or submersion, even when a model has a water- or sweat-resistance rating. We highly recommend using headphones specifically designed and rated for swimming in a pool or open water instead. Water resistance is intended to help with sweat, rain or splashes and is not the same as a tested depth-and-duration rating for immersion.
 If your priority is exercise outside the pool, AirPods may still suit your needs. See TechRadar’s best workout headphones guide for options aimed at running, gym sessions and other land-based training.

And for long sessions, the Suunto Aqua’s 10 hours of audio playback can be boosted to a total of 30 hours with the portable powerbank.

 Want to listen to music without completely tuning out the world? The best bone conduction headphones let you do exactly that, keeping your ears open while you listen to music, podcasts or whatever else you need to hear. They sit against your cheekbones rather than in your ears, using vibrations to send sound to your inner ear.
 That makes them particularly appealing for runners, cyclists and anyone who likes to hear what's happening around them while they exercise. We’ve run, worked out and spent plenty of time testing these headphones ourselves, so we know that the best pair isn't simply the one with the loudest sound or the longest battery life. Comfort, stability and how well you can actually hear your surroundings matter just as much when you're halfway through a run.
 They can be useful outside exercise, too. The open-ear design means you can listen at your desk without completely shutting out your colleagues, or use them for general listening when you don't want earbuds in your ears. 
If you're looking for a pair for swimming, you'll need to pay particular attention to water resistance and how the headphones store music, as Bluetooth doesn't work underwater. Some models can handle both land and water, which is handy if you want one pair for multi-sport training. We’ve highlighted the waterproof options in our lineup, so you can easily spot which ones are suitable for the pool. If swimming is your main priority, you may also want to take a look at our best swimming headphones guide for more options.

 There are compromises, though. Bone conduction headphones generally can't match good earbuds for sound quality, and some models leak sound at higher volumes. We’ll flag those limitations rather than glossing over them, so you can work out whether bone conduction is actually right for you before spending your money.
 Below, you'll find the best bone conduction headphones we've tested, from models suited to running and everyday listening to waterproof options for the pool. We regularly update this guide as we test new models throughout 2026.
 Disclaimer

 Are bone conduction headphones good for swimming? 
 (Image credit: Shokz) If you need completely swimproof bone conduction headphones, you'll need a pair rated IP68 or higher 
 Water doesn't conduct Bluetooth signals well, so you'll also need onboard music storage 
 If you’re thinking about investing in a pair of bone conduction headphones for use while swimming, then be sure to check the IP (ingress protection) rating, which will provide an indication of how well they'll be able to fend off sweat and water.
 Generally, an IP68 or higher rating ensures total protection in water. In the list above, that's the H20 Tri 2 Pro, Nank RunnerDiver 2 Pro, Jabees 7Seven and Shokz OpenSwim Pro. The Shokz OpenRun 2 Pro are not designed for the pool, although they are sweat- and rain-resistant.
 Bluetooth signals also don't travel well underwater, which is why headphones designed for swimming feature built-in music storage. Our best swimming headphones guide can tell you more. It's also about charging method: plugs are tough to keep water out of, while magnetic chargers are easier.
 (Image credit: Future) Are bone conduction headphones safer? 
 Bone conduction headphones keep you aware of your surroundings 
 They leave your ears free so you can hear pedestrians, traffic and other athletes 
 Generally, yes. Similar to transparency modes on some ANC headphones, bone conduction headphones allow ambient sound to reach your ears. However, the difference here is that rather than use the built-in microphones in in-ear buds, bone conduction headphones don't plug up your ears at all.
 This is why many organized race events prohibit the use of headphones other than bone conduction or open-ear headsets. Earbuds that leave your ears open are becoming more common too, and we have a dedicated guide to the best open earbuds .
 Do bone conduction headphones sound good? 
 Bone conduction headphones have reasonable-to-good sound quality 
 Because your ears are exposed to external sound, you're never going to get sound quality comparable to the best in-ear or over-ear headphones 
 Bone conduction headphones still sound great for running, with satisfying bass 
 All of the bone conduction headphones in this guide offer decent audio performance, but you're never going to get the same sound quality as you would from a pair of in-ear headphones or over-ear headphones .
 If you do want to stay aware of your surroundings without sacrificing audio quality, there are plenty of true wireless earbuds out there with transparency modes, which feed in sound from the outside world to your ears.
 Are there any health benefits to using bone conduction headphones? 
 There is no evidence that bone conduction headphones are more or less damaging to your eardrums than in-ear headphones 
 Bone conduction headphones do present a better safety prospect 
 This is because you can also hear your surroundings while you listen to music or podcasts, increasing your spatial awareness in public 
 There's a theory that bone conduction headphones could be better for your hearing health than earbuds, over-ear, and on-ear headphones . That's because they're not driving air directly to your eardrum, which can lead to damage if you listen to music at loud volumes.
 However, studies have shown there is no difference in pressure on the ear canal between bone conduction and in-ear headphones.

 Bone conduction headphones do work for swimming, but only if the model you buy has a genuine submersion rating and onboard music storage. Bluetooth audio dies the instant your head goes under, so every swim-worthy pair in this guide runs its own MP3 player while the Bluetooth radio handles your dry-land training. We spent 2026 season logging laps with twelve sets so you can pick the right one before you take it to the pool deck.
 Our answer for most swimmers is the SHOKZ OpenSwim Pro, which pairs an IP68 rating with 32GB of internal memory and a dedicated swim EQ mode. If that is more headset than you need, the PSIER S18 gives you the same 32GB onboard library for a fraction of the outlay, and the VLOP VP01 adds a hybrid driver that sounds noticeably fuller than most bone conduction designs.
 There is one thing to clear up before anything else: swimming headphones are not the same as the bone conduction running headphones most people already own. A sweat-rated fitness band has no submersion rating at all, and neither do AirPods or any other sealed earbud. Swim-specific means IPX7 or better, a sealed build, and a music source that does not need a radio signal. The same open-ear design that keeps your ear canals clear, so you can hear a lifeguard or a coach, is also what makes it usable around a pool at all.

 Save this one for occasional beach and holiday swimming where the low cost absorbs the risk. For a committed training schedule, the extra outlay on a set with stronger seals and a longer track record is money well spent.

 Buying Guide: How Swim Headphones Actually Work
 Every question we get about swim headphones comes down to a handful of technical facts. Get these right and the twelve sets above sort themselves into tiers you can actually choose between.
 What IP ratings really mean for a swimmer
 An ingress protection code has two digits and they are not additive. The first covers solids, so 6 means dust-tight. The second covers water, and it is the only part that matters in a pool.
 An X in that position means the rating was not tested, which is why IPX8 is common and tells you nothing about dust. IPX7 means immersion to 1 metre for 30 minutes. IPX8 means continuous submersion deeper than 1 metre for a duration set by the manufacturer, usually 2 metres for 1 or 2 hours. IP69 adds resistance to high-pressure, high-temperature water jets.
 The trap is that IPX8 is not a single standard. Two different brands can both print IPX8 and mean anything from 2 metres for 1 hour to 5 metres for 2.5 hours, which is why the depth and time figures printed next to the rating matter more than the rating itself. For open water, treat the label as a starting point and rinse in fresh water afterwards.
 Why Bluetooth drops the moment you submerge
 Water absorbs and scatters radio waves, and human tissue is a dense and lossy medium for a 2.4GHz signal. A phone on the pool deck may be 3 metres from your head and your connection will still collapse the instant you push off the wall.
 That is why every headset above carries onboard storage. The MP3 player is the real audio source in the pool, Bluetooth is a land-use feature, and any listing that leads with Bluetooth as the headline for swimming is describing a product that will go silent underwater.
 How to wear swimming headphones so they stay put
 Fit is decided in about fifteen seconds and most problems trace back to skipping it.
 Ear hooks on first. Seat both transducers just in front of the ear, on the cheekbone rather than the temple, before anything else goes on.
 Cap over the top. Pull a silicone swim cap down over the frame so the cap holds the hooks rather than competing with them.
 Goggles strap check. Put the goggle strap on after the headphones and confirm the two do not fight for the same spot above the ear.
 Tether to the goggles. Clip the short cord from the band to the goggle strap so a dropped set surfaces.
 Dry check. Press play underwater before you settle into a set, so you know MP3 mode is active before you are 200 metres out.
 MP3 storage, Bluetooth or a poolside transmitter
 There are three ways to get sound into the water and only one of them works with no setup at all.
 Onboard MP3 is the standard here. You build a library on your computer, transfer it by cable or magnetic dock, and the headset plays it with no phone in sight. It is the only option that works in open water, and it is why every pick above has storage. The cost is that you manage files rather than playlists.
 Bluetooth handles your dry-land training and nothing else. Treat it as a road running feature on a swim headset.
 A poolside transmitter relays audio over a short radio link from a base unit on the deck, which lets you play a stream without preparing files. It is genuinely convenient for pool-only swimmers, and it usually sits behind a subscription, so the running cost is the part to compare against a one-time device. For open water there is no base unit, so it is not an option at all.
 One workflow worth flagging: features that record a streaming playlist to the device sit in a grey area against most streaming services’ terms of use. Check your provider’s current policy before building a library that way.
 Earplugs change underwater clarity more than any EQ setting
 This is the highest-leverage trick in the whole guide and it is free. Without earplugs, water rushing past the open ear canal produces a roar that masks everything, and you turn the volume up to compensate until speech becomes muddy.
 A fitted silicone swim plug blocks the canal, stops the rush, and evens out the perceived volume between strokes. Owners consistently report that podcasts go from impossible to followable. Most of the sets above include a pair, and if yours did not, budget for a multi-pair pack.
 The technique matters as much as the plug. Roll it small, pull the ear upward and back to open the canal, and hold it in place for several seconds before you let go. A plug that is too big falls out on the dive and one that is too small never seals.
 How to clean and dry a swim headset after every session
 Post-swim care is the single most skipped step, and it decides whether the seals last a season or three.
 Rinse in fresh water. After open water or a salty pool, hold the headset under a fresh tap for 30 seconds so salt does not crystallise in the port covers.
 Check the port covers. Wipe the charging contacts and the sealing surfaces before they dry, since trapped salt is abrasive.
 Air dry fully, uncovered. Leave the headset out of any case until there is no moisture in the ear hooks. Charging a damp device is a common accidental failure.
 Wipe the silicone down. A damp cloth clears chlorine film from the cushions, which otherwise degrades the material.
 The honest downsides of bone conduction in the pool
 Five drawbacks come up consistently, and knowing them in advance prevents most returns.
 Bass is weak. A cheekbone does not transmit low frequencies well, so every open-ear swim headset sounds thinner than an in-ear alternative. Hybrid designs mitigate this rather than solving it.
 Bluetooth does not work underwater. This is physics, and it catches out almost every new owner at least once.
 Ear hooks get sore on long swims. Reports of pressure and soreness past an hour or two appear across every hooked design, and hook-free frames exist for exactly this reason.
 Preparing a library is a chore. Streaming services do not transfer to these devices, so the first session is usually a file-transfer project.
 They are not quieter than the water. Open ears help with a lifeguard or a coach, but in heavy chop with waves you will not hear a boat.
 On that last point, a straight answer to the question swimmers keep asking: swimming with audio in open water is a real safety trade. Bone conduction is safer than sealed earbuds because your ear canals stay open, and safer than swimming with nothing only in the sense that you remain partly aware. It is not a substitute for swimming within your sight of shore or a buddy when conditions are poor.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 What are the best bone conduction headphones for swimming?
 For most swimmers the SHOKZ OpenSwim Pro is the best all-round choice, because it combines an IP68 rating for submersion to 2 metres for 2 hours with 32GB of onboard storage and a dedicated swim EQ mode. The PSIER S18 offers the same 32GB library at a much lower outlay, and the VLOP VP01 is worth considering if fuller sound matters more to you, since its hybrid bone plus air conduction driver keeps more low end than a pure bone conduction design.
 Do bone conduction headphones work for swimming?
 Yes, but only models rated for submersion, and only with onboard music storage. Bone conduction transducers sit on your cheekbone, so nothing blocks your ear canal, which is also why you can still hear a lifeguard. The catch is audio delivery: water absorbs Bluetooth radio signals, so a phone connection drops the moment you submerge and the headset has to play MP3 files from internal memory.
 What IP rating do I need for swimming headphones?
 IPX7 or higher, and check the printed depth and duration rather than the code alone. IPX7 means immersion to 1 metre for 30 minutes. IPX8 means continuous submersion deeper than 1 metre for a manufacturer-defined time, commonly 2 metres for 1 or 2 hours. IP68 adds a dust rating. Because IPX8 is not a single standard, two brands can both print it and mean very different limits.
 Can you use Bluetooth headphones while swimming?
 No. Water absorbs and scatters the 2.4GHz radio signal a Bluetooth connection relies on, so audio cuts out as soon as your head submerges, even with your phone sitting on the pool deck metres away. Every swim headset worth buying has a dual mode, with Bluetooth handling runs and cycling on land while an internal MP3 player handles the pool.
 What is the downside of bone conduction headphones for swimming?
 Five things come up repeatedly. Bass is weak because a cheekbone does not transmit low frequencies, so everything sounds thinner than in-ear buds. Bluetooth is inert underwater. Ear hooks and headbands get sore past an hour or two on long swims. Preparing a music library takes time, because streaming services do not transfer to these devices. And open ears are not silent, so in heavy chop you will not hear a boat.
 Which Bone Conduction Headphones Should You Buy?
 The SHOKZ OpenSwim Pro is the best bone conduction headphone for swimming in 2026 for anyone who wants one headset to handle the pool, the run and the bike, and its IP68 rating with 32GB of storage covers the widest range of swimming conditions of anything we tested. If the outlay is the deciding factor, the PSIER S18 gives you the same storage and a proven chlorine-durability record for far less, at the cost of a stiffer band and a shorter warranty.
 Choose the CXK X17 for the largest transducer and the longest battery, the ZOVIMAX X7 MAX if you swim in deeper open water, the Tevese X9 if ear hooks are a dealbreaker, and the MARLALL X26 if you surf or swim in conditions that test retention. Whichever you settle on, fit the earplugs, put the cap over the hooks, and rinse the headset in fresh water afterwards. That routine does more for how good your swim sounds than any specification on the box.
